what: Findability for newsroom.sgit.ai, derived by admin/build/find.py from newsroom/wire.json, the articles' markdown twins and admin/content/find/find-editorial.json. Desks by audience, a controlled vocabulary, series in reading order, a format and a reading time per article. Edit the editorial file, not this one.

rule.desks: Each controlled tag belongs to one desk. An article scores 3 for the desk of its first controlled tag, 2 for its second and 1 for each further one, plus its topics (first 2, others 1; Graphs & knowledge counts for Vaults, Site & engineering for Building). The highest score is the primary desk, the runner-up the secondary. An editor override replaces the rule and says why. A call is debatable when the runner-up scores at least 80% of the winner, or when it was overridden.
rule.tags: Near-duplicates and plurals merge into one subject. Format words become the format label. Our own products are never subject tags. Tags that apply to most of the newsroom are rejected: the desk does that job. A raw tag the editor has not mapped is listed under unmapped and waits for the Librarian.
rule.series: Two or more articles that tell one story in order; each later part builds on an earlier one.
rule.formats: An editor override; else a raw format tag; else a cue in the title or teaser; else Analysis.
rule.minutes: words / 230, measured on the markdown twin from the first h2 to Threads.

desks.label: Agent security & policy
desks.for_whom: For security leads, risk owners and boards deciding what an agent may do and who carries the risk.

start_here.why: Start with the idea the rest stands on: a risk exists the moment the exposure does, so the only question is who accepted it.
Then the two words this desk uses most, defined: what an agent did, and what its reach could cost.
A real six-agent setup, rule by rule, graded by what actually enforces each one today.
The argument measured: one customer service agent built three ways, and how much of each policy is only hope.
Where the desk had got to by 11 October: Satya Nadella's seven principles, answered with what runs and what is still design.

desks.label: Building with agents
desks.for_whom: For engineers and builders running agents day to day: tools, memory, email, desktops and review.

start_here.why: Begin where the team began: one Claude session with a policy, then roles talking in files, in phases you can copy.
Why the agents moved off the laptop, and the two walls an operating system gives you.
A year of daily practice in one guide: a session per topic, named agents, curated memory.
What happened when a written rule was not enough, and the hook that now checks every draft.
The warning that follows: when every mistake adds a rule, complexity wins, and the way back to shipping.

desks.label: Vaults & provenance
desks.for_whom: For anyone who needs evidence they can open: encrypted vaults, keys, graphs and the publishing method.

start_here.why: The shortest way in: git for the files you cannot put on GitHub, encrypted before they leave your machine.
The method, from the first fortnight of August, where every rule exists because something went wrong first.
The other idea the site keeps returning to: graphs with no privileged level and no shared schema.
Why the vaults matter to a stranger: proof a reader can open, and what happens when it sits two clicks away.
Where the method stands now: no database, no back end, and servers that cannot read your data.

desks.label: The future of news
desks.for_whom: For editors, journalists and publishers asking how news gets paid for when agents do the reading.

start_here.why: The founding argument: the story is a graph of claims and evidence, and the article is one view of it.
The history behind it: the reader was always the product, from 1833 to AI taking the traffic.
The idea made concrete on one local story, followed to the end and paid back to its sources.
The newsroom tries it on itself: a penny a page, from credit kept in your browser.
Where the argument lands on 11 October: agents will pay to read, because it is cheaper than not paying.

desks.label: Strategy & startups
desks.for_whom: For founders and investors: pricing, early access, Wardley maps and who pays for open source.

start_here.why: The startup question this desk keeps asking first: would anybody miss it if you took it away?
The next step: price it, then give it away to people who know you, and measure what it costs them.
A Wardley-style reading of the SaaS shake-out: inertia decides, not the AI.
Who pays for the long tail, measured from public data, with five ways to pay simulated.
The founder answering ten hard questions about the company: what it does, and what it deliberately is not.
